Nine plugins, a terminal UI, the fixes from two audits, and a compose stack
that drives every core plugin end to end. Both modules build on Go 1.27.

## Upgrading

Four changes want a look at the config before the new binary goes live:

- Relayed requests are dropped unless `relay: allow ...` is in that family's
  chain. A DHCPv4 reply goes wherever the sender wrote giaddr, so the server
  no longer answers relays it was never told about
- `relayinfo` requires an `allow` list of relay addresses, spelled the way
  `relay` spells it
- `metrics` binds loopback or a unix socket only; a wildcard or routable bind
  is refused at startup
- `range` and `range6` turn away new leases past `max-leases`, 65536 by
  default; 0 removes the bound

Smaller ones: the config search order puts the working directory last, so
`/etc/coredhcp/config.yml` wins over one next to the binary. The `sleep`
plugin is out of both default binaries. Hook programs started by `leasehook`
get an allow-listed environment (PATH, HOME, TMPDIR, LANG, LC_\*) instead of
the server's, and a webhook redirect is refused. The image runs as uid 65532
with file capabilities, which `no-new-privileges` and
`allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` ignore; the README's Docker section says
what to do then. Names `ddns` wrote before this release carry no DHCID and
are adopted by the first client that asks for them; `protect:` covers the
ones that matter.

## Added

- Nine plugins upstream does not have: relay (drop relayed requests from
  relays not on the list, and a RELEASE whose ciaddr is not the address it
  came from), ratelimit (a token bucket per client, keyed by MAC, source or
  both), subnet (several scopes from one server, chosen by relay address,
  interface or the address the client holds; each scope in one YAML file),
  range6 (DHCPv6 addresses from a pool, in sqlite across restarts), relayinfo
  (addresses by the port a request came in on, from option 82 or the relay's
  interface-id), bootfile (a boot program per client architecture, with an
  iPXE entry), ddns (RFC 2136 updates signed with TSIG, names held with a
  DHCID record, delivery off the packet path), leasehook (every lease event
  to a webhook or a program as JSON, optionally HMAC-signed) and leaseapi
  (`/v1/leases`, `/v1/pools` and `/v1/health` read-only on a unix socket or
  loopback)
- coredhcp-tui: the server with a screen in front of it. Sockets, the plugin
  chain per family with how often each plugin answered or dropped, every
  exchange as it is handled, offered and confirmed leases, counters, the
  request rate and the log. A module of its own under cmd/, so tview and
  tcell stay out of the root go.mod; it ships as a second binary per
  platform below. `make demo` runs it against busybox clients in compose
- Plugins can ask which interface a datagram arrived on and where it came
  from (`Setup4Ctx`, `Setup6Ctx`, `handler.RequestInfoFrom`). A chain of
  plugins that do not ask pays nothing
- `file` and `redis` key leases on the DUID or the option 61 client
  identifier with `key:duid` and `key:client-id`; a MAC is the wrong key for
  a DUID-EN or DUID-UUID client
- `make test-all`: all 29 core plugins on both families in compose with
  Knot, Redis, a mocked NetBox and a webhook receiver, 49 scenarios on-link
  and relayed. `make test-ddns` runs the ddns plugin against a real Knot.
  Both run in CI
- Every plugin documents itself in doc.go, arguments, defaults, what a wrong
  value does at startup and where it goes in the chain; `go generate
  ./plugins/` renders each one to a README in the plugin directory and CI
  fails when one lags. The main README gets a plugin-order section

## Fixed

Inherited from upstream unless noted:

- A DHCPv4 RELEASE or DECLINE is never answered and runs the plugin chain;
  DECLINE reaches the plugins in both families
- `range` no longer allocates on a RELEASE from a client it has never seen,
  releases only on a matching ciaddr, and holds a declined address back for a
  bounded time
- `prefix` expires and reclaims delegations, answers RELEASE and caps what
  one packet may claim
- `server_id` decides on option 54 rather than siaddr and requires it on
  RELEASE and DECLINE
- `nbp` added option 59 once per ORO entry, so one Solicit built a 2 MB reply
- `ddns` holds each name against the client it was written for and ignores a
  release for a name it did not register, so one client cannot take or
  delete another's
- `ipv6only` answered a DHCPRELEASE and ended the chain, `relayinfo` added a
  second IA_NA next to range6's, and `staticroute` panicked on an IPv6 route
  when the reply was encoded; it refuses one at setup now
- The `file` and `relayinfo` watchers drain the fsnotify error channel and
  watch the directory, so a reload no longer stops silently
- `range` and `range6` write sqlite off the plugin lock and answer only after
  the write. In-flight handlers are bounded, eight per processor by default,
  and a datagram that finds them all busy is dropped and counted rather
  than queued
- An empty `listen` list is refused instead of panicking (fork-specific), a
  dying listener exits non-zero, and a failed bind no longer strands the
  read loops already started
- Plugin secrets, the TSIG key included, are redacted in the startup log and
  in the terminal UI, and a `?` in a sqlite path can no longer set
  connection options (fork-specific)

## Changed

- Go 1.27 in both modules; CI tests the release the module requires and no
  other
- Every error, warning and HTTP error body that reaches an operator says
  what is wrong and what to do about it
- One lint config for both modules, 26 more linters at zero findings, and
  comments cut down to the why
- The release workflow pins every action to a SHA and publishes the image
  with provenance, an SBOM and a cosign signature; the README shows how to
  verify one
- 96.5% statement coverage in the root module outside the compose
  exerciser, 100% in the terminal UI

## Container image

Multi-arch (linux/amd64, linux/arm64), signed:

    docker run --rm ghcr.io/hyperized/coredhcp:0.3.0 -P
    docker run --rm --net host \
        -v /etc/coredhcp:/etc/coredhcp:ro \
        ghcr.io/hyperized/coredhcp:0.3.0

The entrypoint reads /etc/coredhcp/config.yaml; the server needs the host
network to share a broadcast domain with its clients. The terminal UI is not
in the image; take the `coredhcp-tui-linux-*` binary below.
